d: From a fresh VPS to a Laravel app on HTTPS in five commands.
x: From a fresh Ubuntu server to a Laravel app on HTTPS, in about fifteen minutes. Every step shows the real command and what it prints; click a terminal to jump to the end. Install one command on the server Log in as cipi, with your SSH key Create an app isolated user, DB, PHP Deploy zero downtime from Git HTTPS Let's Encrypt, auto-renewed You need: an Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 VPS with a public IP, a domain whose DNS you control, and a Git repository. Cipi is free; the only cost is the server. 1. Install Cipi SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your

SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your SSH public key, shows its plan, then installs and hardens the whole stack. $ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash Save the credentials it prints. Requirements, SSH keys and unattended installs: Install Cipi .
Root login over SSH is now off. Connect as cipi with your key and prefix commands with sudo (no password needed for cipi ). $ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10 $ sudo cipi status

The wizard asks for the app type, runtime, database, name, domain and repository, then builds an isolated app: its own Linux user, database, PHP pool, Nginx vhost, worker and deploy key. $ sudo cipi app create Skip the questions with flags: sudo cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --branch=main The summary at the end (database password, deploy key, webhook token, a mariadb+ssh:// URL for TablePlus or DBeaver) is shown once . Save it.

If you gave the installer a Git token, there is nothing to do: Cipi added the deploy key and the push webhook to the repository. Otherwise add the ssh-ed25519 … key from the summary as a read-only deploy key : Provider Where GitHub Repository → Settings → Deploy keys GitLab Settings → Repository → Deploy keys Bitbucket Repository settings → Access keys Azure DevOps User settings → SSH public keys Then check that the server can read it: sudo cipi git check myapp . Tokens and automatic setup: Git providers .

Cipi keeps cache, sessions and queues in each app's own database , so no app can read another's data. Laravel 11+ ships those tables; on an older project create them once and commit: php artisan cache:table && php artisan session:table && php artisan queue:table Migrations run on every deploy. Prefer Valkey for speed or Horizon? Switch per app in Valkey .

$ sudo cipi deploy myapp The new release is built in its own folder, migrated, then made live with one atomic symlink swap. Visitors never see a half-deployed app, and cipi deploy myapp --rollback goes back in a second. How it works: Deploy & roll back .

Point the domain's DNS at the server, then: $ sudo cipi ssl install myapp The certificate covers the domain and its aliases and renews itself. Behind the Cloudflare proxy use --dns=cloudflare and set SSL/TLS to Full (strict) . More in SSL certificates .

Prefer a browser, or need one for clients? Install the API and the panel, each on its own domain. The panel can manage this server and any other Cipi server you connect. $ sudo cipi api api.example.com $ sudo cipi gui panel.example.com

d: The stack Cipi installs and how each app is laid out on disk.
x: Cipi is a command-line tool that lives on your server. It installs a proven open-source stack, then creates and runs apps on it, each one sealed off from the others. There is no external service in the loop: no account, no agent phoning home, nothing to pay. The server Nginx web server, TLS, proxy PHP-FPM / Octane several PHP versions side by side MariaDB / PostgreSQL one database per app Valkey cache, queues (opt-in per app) Supervisor workers, Horizon, Reverb Component Role Nginx (nginx.org mainline) Web server, reverse proxy, TLS termination, HTTP/2 hardening PHP-FPM PHP runtime per app; 8.

d: Run apps on FrankenPHP, convert existing apps and pin builds.
x: Laravel Octane keeps your app booted in memory and serves requests with FrankenPHP. Typical result: much lower response times for the same hardware. Octane and PHP-FPM apps run side by side on one server. Create or convert Your repository needs laravel/octane , installed with php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first deploy. cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane cipi app convert myapp --to=octane # an existing FPM app cipi app convert myapp --to=fpm # and back cipi app limits myapp --octane-work

Your repository needs laravel/octane , installed with php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first deploy. cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane cipi app convert myapp --to=octane # an existing FPM app cipi app convert myapp --to=fpm # and back cipi app limits myapp --octane-workers=4

Nginx static files, proxy to Octane Octane on 127.0.0.1 port 8100–8999 FrankenPHP build pinned per app Supervisor keeps it running, reloads on deploy Piece Setting Nginx proxy_pass to the app's local port; static files from current/public ; no PHP-FPM pool Process Supervisor program myapp-octane , next to the queue workers Deploys The pinned FrankenPHP binary is linked into each release, then Octane reloads .env OCTANE_SERVER=frankenphp , OCTANE_HTTPS=true Converting rewrites the vhost, process, deploy recipe and .env , and keeps the certificate. It turns JIT off; enable it again if you use it.

The PHP an Octane app runs is the one compiled into its FrankenPHP binary. Cipi keeps those binaries in /opt/cipi-frankenphp/builds/ (read-only to apps) and pins one per app . A deploy never downloads a new binary, so PHP changes only when you decide. cipi frankenphp # each app's build and PHP, patched or not cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp # newest build on the same PHP minor cipi frankenphp upgrade --all cipi frankenphp use myapp # pin a specific build cipi frankenphp import ./frankenphp # a build you compiled (other PHP minor) cipi frankenphp adopt myapp # pin the binary Octane downloaded cipi frankenphp prune # remove unused builds Rule Why it keeps you stable Upgrades stay on the app's PHP minor and FrankenPHP major No surprise PHP 8.5 → 8.6 jump Octane must answer after an upgrade, or the previous build returns A bad build never stays live A deploy that needs a newer FrankenPHP stops before migrations The live release is untouched; run cipi frankenphp upgrade Apps on different PHP minors use different builds 8.5 and 8.6 coexist Nightly patches via cipi autoupdate (component frankenphp ) Security fixes without manual work To move an app to a new PHP minor: cipi app edit myapp --php=8.6 , then cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp . Octane serves HTTP only. Run long jobs on queue workers or Horizon and WebSockets on Reverb .

d: Turn the OPcache JIT on or off for a single app.
x: PHP's JIT compiles hot code to machine code. It helps CPU-bound work (calculations, big collections, heavy templating) and does little for requests that mostly wait on the database. Cipi turns it on for one app , FPM or Octane, and checks it before and after. cipi app jit myapp on # tracing mode, 128M buffer cipi app jit myapp on --mode=function --buffer=256M cipi app jit myapp off cipi app jit myapp --json # current state Check When If it fails PHP can start with JIT (no Xdebug/pcov, JIT compiled in) Before Refused, nothing written PHP-FPM active / Octane answering After Previous setting rest

d: SPA, static and SSR frontends built on every deploy.
x: Node apps build and serve modern front-ends with the same lifecycle as Laravel apps: releases, rollback, webhook, SSL, basic auth, redirects, proxies and the deploy audit. # Vite SPA: build, serve dist/ with an index.html fallback cipi app create --user=web --domain=web.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/web.git --node=spa --framework=vite # Pre-rendered site (Astro, Nuxt generate, Next export) cipi app create --user=docs --domain=docs.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/docs.git --node=static --output=dist # Node server with blue/green deploys cipi app create --user=shop

Mode Nginx Use for spa Serves the build; unknown paths fall back to /index.html Client-side routed apps static Serves the build; real 404s via /404.html Pre-rendered sites ssr Proxies to a Node process on localhost, WebSockets included Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro SSR Hashed assets ( assets/ , _astro/ , _nuxt/ , _app/immutable/ ) are cached as immutable; HTML is never cached.

Flag Meaning --framework Preset: vite (spa), next , nuxt , sveltekit , astro , remix (ssr). Explicit flags win --node-version LTS major: 22 or 24 (default: the server default ) --build Build command (default npm run build ) --start SSR start command, a Node runner plus arguments, e.g. node build --output Build folder for spa/static; the deploy fails if it has no index.html --health-path SSR path that must answer below 500 before a release takes traffic (default / ) The build installs from your lockfile ( npm ci , pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , yarn install --immutable , bun install --frozen-lockfile ) with NODE_ENV=production . shared/.env is read at build time and by SSR servers at runtime; edit it with cipi app env .

Start new release on the idle slot Health check must answer < 500 in 60 s Switch upstream nginx -t, reload Drain old slot then stop it Two Supervisor programs ( shop-node-blue , shop-node-green ) each own a local port. If the new release crashes or never answers, it is stopped, the old slot keeps serving and the deploy fails before anything goes live. Rollback and cipi node restart switch the same way. The switch runs as root through a narrow rule: ports, start command, Node version and health path come from a root-owned file, not from the app. .env is read as data, never executed; HOST is forced to 127.0.0.1 and the start command runs without a shell.

cipi node status shop # mode, commands, slots cipi node restart shop # zero downtime cipi node logs shop --lines=100 cipi app edit shop --start="node .output/server/index.mjs" --health-path=/health cipi app edit web --node=static --output=dist The same settings can live in your repository in the node: section of cipi.yml . Push-to-deploy works without a Laravel agent: Cipi ships a hardened webhook receiver that verifies GitHub/Bitbucket signatures and GitLab/Azure tokens. Node apps get no database by default; add one with cipi db . cipi sync and cipi app clone do not handle Node apps yet.

cipi worker horizon enable myapp cipi worker horizon status myapp cipi worker horizon disable myapp Horizon replaces the queue:work workers of that app (one or the other, not both). It needs the queues on Redis: set QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis with cipi app env ; each app has its own Valkey instance ready. When a deploy finds laravel/horizon installed, it helps without overriding your choices: The deploy finds It does Horizon, queues on Redis, no worker Enables Horizon Horizon plus existing workers Explains how to switch; changes nothing Horizon, queues not on Redis Tells you which variable to set A Horizon you disabled stays disabled. cipi pending lists apps with Horizon installed but nothing processing jobs.

Stop workers before the symlink swap Swap release atomic Restart workers on the new code Workers never run old code against a new database. Supervisor restarts a worker only after an unexpected exit. Workers can also be declared in cipi.yml .
App users manage their own workers without root, through a narrow helper: sudo cipi-worker status myapp sudo cipi-worker restart myapp

d: The Laravel scheduler and each app user's crontab.

Nginx is excluded from unattended upgrades so it never restarts unexpectedly. When a new minor comes out, the extension packages ( redis , memcached , imagick ) follow a few days later. Cipi handles the gap: Situation Cipi PHP packaged, some extensions not yet Installs it, records what's missing, adds each extension as soon as it's published (nightly) Only a release candidate available Installs it and labels it prerelease Assigning a version still missing extensions Refused with the list of what's missing; --force if the app doesn't use them A lock file that rejects the new PHP The deploy fails and the live release stays: update the dependency, commit, deploy

PHP is excluded from Ubuntu's unattended upgrades: Cipi patches it itself every night at 03:30 , restarts only the affected PHP-FPM services and reports the result. cipi php upgrade # patch now and print the patch level State Meaning patched At or past the latest security release Cipi knows VULNERABLE A fix exists but isn't installed yet (exit code 1; the nightly job alerts until fixed) distro Ubuntu build: fixes backported without a version bump END OF LIFE No more fixes from PHP: move apps off it prerelease Release candidate, not compared Octane apps run the PHP inside their FrankenPHP binary, which apt never touches; cipi php upgrade lists them too and cipi frankenphp upgrade fixes them.

Every pool Cipi writes (apps, webhook receivers, panel) locks down settings that recent PHP advisories used as attack paths, and Octane apps load the same rules: php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off They are set as admin flags, so neither .user.ini nor ini_set() can turn them back on. d: HTTP checks per app, including after every deploy.
x: Since v5.0 , configure HTTP healthchecks per app. Cipi then watches the app in two different ways, because “is the site up?” and “did the push I just made break production?” are not the same question. Check When it runs When it alerts Periodic probe Every 5 minutes After 3 consecutive failures → health_fail Post-deploy check Right after every release goes live Immediately on the first failure → deploy_health_fail cipi health set myapp --url=https://myapp.com/up --expect=200 cipi health check myapp cipi health list cipi health unset myapp # Structured output (v5.0.6+) — panel API / scripts cipi

Once an app has a healthcheck URL, the release that just went live is verified right after every deploy — from cipi deploy and from the Git webhook alike. The probe waits a short grace period (8 seconds for Octane apps, 3 otherwise, or whatever --grace=N says) and retries five times, so an app that needs a moment to come up is not reported as broken. The verdict never changes the deploy's exit code — the release is live either way — but the alert says so and hands you the rollback command. The success email is sent after verification, so it can never announce a successful deploy while the site is returning 500. Since v5.8.4 a failed verdict also says where the check comes from — cipi health set , the panel's "Enable healthcheck", or a health: block in cipi.yml — and how to change it: --url= , --no-postdeploy to keep the five-minute probe but skip the one after deploys, cipi health unset to remove it. A 404 adds the usual cause: Laravel serves /up only when the health route is on ( bootstrap/app.php , health: '/up' ). cipi health set <app> --no-postdeploy on its own keeps the URL and status already set (before 5.8.4 it reset them to https://<domain>/up and 200). cipi health postdeploy myapp # run the post-deploy verification now cipi health set myapp --grace=15 # give the release longer to warm up (max 120) cipi health set myapp --no-postdeploy # turn the post-deploy check off for this app

Cipi can undo a release that fails its post-deploy healthcheck: the current symlink moves back to the previous release, the app is probed again, and one email describes the whole sequence — what was published, what it answered, what it was rolled back to and whether that fixed it. cipi health set myapp --rollback-on-unhealthy # permanent, per app cipi deploy myapp --rollback-on-unhealthy # just this deploy Four outcomes are reported distinctly: recovered ; rolled back but still unhealthy (so the cause is probably not the code); the rollback itself failed (the bad release is still live); and there is no earlier release to return to. Auto-rollback is off by default and deliberately so: database migrations are not undone. A release that migrated the schema and then failed can be worse off after the code is rolled back. Enable it only for apps whose deploys do not migrate, or where you know the migrations are backwards-compatible. REST: GET /api/health , GET|PUT|DELETE /api/apps/{name}/health , POST /api/apps/{name}/health/check (API 1.15.0+ / Cipi 5.0.6+ ). An app can also declare its healthcheck in its repository — see cipi.yml . To watch the server rather than the app — disk, services, workers, 5xx spikes, load — see cipi monitor (v5.3.0+).

h: Edge-triggered, so the cron never spams

http_5xx keeps a byte offset per log, so it only reads what was written since the last run. The offsets survive logrotate, and the first run only records a baseline — it never alerts on last week's errors. load needs runs consecutive runs over the limit: a single 5-minute spike is noise, a sustained one is a problem. app_disk walks app homes with du , so it measures only apps that have a limit and reuses a measurement for minutes ( 30 by default): the 5-minute cron does not walk every home each time. A manual cipi monitor measures afresh. Each app keeps its own alert state, so a second app going over is not hidden behind the first, and a recovery follows when an app is back under its limit. A check that cannot run reports crit instead of crashing the runner. Every check maps to its own trigger, so any of them can be muted like everything else: cipi notifications disable monitor_load . Alerts go out through the normal notification path: email once cipi smtp configure is done, and every chat channel you add. It prints every local filesystem, then every app, largest first, in GB and as a share of the disk. The same reading from your laptop is cipi-cli disk ( cipi-cli 1.6.0+ , API 1.33+ , ability disk-view ; the server needs 5.5.2+ so the API may run cipi disk ). cipi disk # the server, then every app cipi disk db # every database, engine by engine, in MB cipi disk --json # same figures for scripts (also: cipi disk db --json) cipi app limits shop --disk=10 # soft limit: alert at 90% and whe

h: cipi disk db — every database, in MB
x: Next to the per-app figure, a listing of the databases themselves, for every engine installed on the server. It shows what the app table cannot: databases that belong to no app, and the engines that are not SQL. MariaDB DATABASE SIZE blog 2.0 MB shop 200.0 MB On disk, whole engine 500.0 MB Valkey DATABASE KEYS SIZE db0 1204 — Memory in use 12.3 MB On disk, whole engine 3.0 MB Meilisearch INDEX DOCUMENTS SIZE shop-products 12000 8.4 MB On disk, whole engine 45.0 MB MariaDB — one row per database, empty ones included. The size is the larger of what the server reports and the database's directory in the data dir, since the files include space the server has not handed back. These are the figures the DATABASE column of cipi disk uses. PostgreSQL — one row per database ( pg_database_size ). Valkey — one row per logical database ( db0 , db1 , …) with its number of keys. Every engine closes with its size on disk as a whole (data directory, logs included). An engine that is installed but does not answer gets a note and still shows that total; an engine that is not installed is left out.

h: A soft disk limit per app
x: No app has a limit until you give it one — the default is unlimited, on new and existing servers alike. A limit is a number of GB for files and database together (the TOTAL column), set with cipi app limits <app> --disk=<GB> . It is soft : nothing is blocked when it is passed and the app keeps working. The limit is a threshold for the app_disk monitor check, which warns at 90% of it, goes critical once the app is over, and sends a recovery when it is back under — through email and every chat channel, trigger monitor_app_disk . A hard limit (filesystem quotas) is deliberately not part of this: it cannot cover the database, needs quotas enabled on the filesystem, and takes a site down when it is reached. The whole-server alert did not change: the disk check has warned at 80% and gone critical at 90% of any filesystem since 5.3.0, on by default.

The key name is resolved via SSH_USER_AUTH with an auth.log fallback when needed.

Cipi integrates PAM-based authentication notifications via pam_exec.so with ExposeAuthInfo enabled. When SMTP is configured, the system automatically sends email alerts on these security-relevant events: Sudo and su elevation — triggered when any user successfully runs sudo or su . The notification includes the username, target user (for su ), the TTY, SSH key, client IP, and timestamp. Privileged SSH login — triggered when root or any user in the sudo group logs in via SSH. The notification includes the username, source IP address, SSH key fingerprint, and key comment (resolved from /var/log/auth.log fingerprint matching against authorized_keys ). SSH key changes — triggered when an SSH key is added to, removed from, or renamed on the cipi user via cipi ssh add , cipi ssh remove , or cipi ssh rename . The notification includes the hostname, server IP, key fingerprint, key comment, timestamp, and remaining key count. Rename alerts also include the old and new key name. App lifecycle events — triggered when an app is created, edited, or deleted. The notification includes the server hostname, app name, domain, and PHP version. Notifications run asynchronously in the background so they never delay login or command execution. If SMTP is not configured, the hooks fail silently with no impact on the system.

Regardless of SMTP configuration, all notification events (SSH key changes, app lifecycle, password resets, sudo/su/SSH login, cron failures) are always logged to /var/log/cipi/events.log in a compact one-line format. The log is rotated daily with 1-year retention via logrotate.
The cipi-cron-notify utility wraps system cron jobs and sends a notification if the job exits with a non-zero code. This is useful for monitoring critical scheduled tasks.

Each channel gets a 5-second timeout , and a failed delivery is only logged to /var/log/cipi/events.log : a slow or dead webhook can never stall a deploy or a cron run. x: Cipi enforces automatic log rotation policies designed to meet GDPR and general data protection requirements. Logs are rotated and deleted automatically — no manual cleanup needed. Category Logs Retention Application Laravel, PHP-FPM, workers, deploy, system 12 months Security Fail2ban, UFW firewall, authentication, Cipi events ( events.log ) 12 months HTTP / Navigation Nginx access and error logs 90 days HTTP/navigation logs (nginx access logs) contain IP addresses, which are personal data under GDPR. The 90-day retention ensures compliance with the data minimization principle while preservin

Up to 5.4 the 12-month policy did not actually reach Laravel logs. Apps were created with LOG_CHANNEL=daily , so every day had its own file, and logrotate rotated each of those files exactly once: the content landed in laravel-<date>.log.1 , which was never compressed ( delaycompress waits for a second rotation that never came) and never deleted ( rotate 365 counts rotations per file, and every date is its own file). Since v5.5.0 Laravel apps write one storage/logs/laravel.log ( LOG_CHANNEL=single ), and the cipi-app-logs rule rotates it daily, compressed from the second day, for 365 rotations. The rule's Laravel pattern is now storage/logs/*[!0-9].log , so a log whose name ends in a date is left to Laravel: an app that sets LOG_CHANNEL=daily on purpose is pruned by Laravel itself after LOG_DAILY_DAYS . The 5.5.0 migration switches existing apps and folds their dated history into laravel.log , from where it leaves through the normal rotation.

During installation, Cipi creates groups cipi-ssh and cipi-apps and applies the following SSH architecture: User Access Method root blocked PermitRootLogin no cipi key-only group cipi-ssh , PasswordAuthentication no globally app users user + password group cipi-apps , Match Group cipi-apps → PasswordAuthentication yes sshd_config uses AllowGroups cipi-ssh cipi-apps instead of AllowUsers . App users can connect with ssh myapp@server-ip and the password generated at app creation. Admin access is via public-key as cipi . SSH keys are managed with cipi ssh list / add / remove — see SSH Key Management . Since v5.5.0, cipi ssh apps disable puts app users in the cipi-nossh group, which a Match Group cipi-nossh Address *,!127.0.0.1,!::1 block denies from every non-local address — deploys over ssh localhost keep working.

Authorized keys for the cipi user can be managed via the CLI with built-in safety: format validation, duplicate prevention, current-session protection, and last-key protection to avoid lockout. When SMTP is configured, every key addition, removal, or rename triggers an email alert with hostname, IP, fingerprint, timestamp, and remaining key count. Rename alerts also include the old and new key name.

Application users are restricted from using su to escalate privileges to root or the cipi account. This is enforced via pam_wheel.so group=sudo , ensuring that only members of the sudo group can switch users.

The www-data user (used by Nginx and PHP-FPM) has its sudoers access restricted to an explicit command whitelist instead of a wildcard pattern. Only the specific /usr/local/bin/cipi subcommands required by the API are allowed. This prevents www-data from running arbitrary commands even if the web application is compromised.
The Cipi API validates every CLI command against an internal whitelist before executing it via sudo . Commands not on the whitelist are rejected, preventing command injection through the API layer.

Each app runs under its own Linux user with chmod 750 on the home directory. No app can read another app's files. PHP-FPM runs each app's pool as the app user with its own Unix socket. cipi app fix-permissions (since v5.2.1 ) restores that layout after a zip unpacked as root or a too-open .ssh : nginx writes vhost logs as www-data into logs/ ( 2775 setgid), the home must stay 750 so www-data (in the app group) can read the docroot, and .ssh must be 700 or OpenSSH StrictModes refuses the deploy key.
open_basedir is configured per FPM pool to restrict PHP to the app's home directory. Even if an app is compromised, PHP cannot access the filesystem outside its own home.

Each app has its own database and user (MariaDB by default; optional PostgreSQL since v4.8.0) with privileges restricted to that database only. A compromised app cannot read or write to another app's database.
Each app gets its own ed25519 SSH key pair. A compromised deploy key only affects one repository — not all apps on the server.

GitHub webhooks are verified using HMAC-SHA256 signatures. GitLab webhooks use token comparison. The webhook handler in cipi-agent returns 200 immediately and writes a flag file — Deployer runs separately as the app user with no elevated privileges.

All Cipi configuration files — server.json , apps.json , databases.json , backup.json , smtp.json , api.json — are encrypted at rest using AES-256-CBC via the built-in Vault system. A per-server master key ( /etc/cipi/.vault_key , chmod 400 ) ensures that even if an attacker gains read access to the filesystem, configuration files containing database passwords, API tokens, and credentials are unreadable without root privileges. See Vault & Encryption for the full architecture.

When transferring applications between servers via cipi sync , the entire archive — including .env files, SSH keys, database dumps, and configuration — is encrypted with AES-256-CBC using a user-provided passphrase. Archives use the .tar.gz.enc extension and cannot be read without the passphrase. This protects sensitive data both at rest (on disk) and in transit (during rsync/scp transfer). See Sync for details.

Cipi enforces automatic log rotation: application and security logs are retained for 12 months, while HTTP/navigation logs (which contain IP addresses — personal data under GDPR) are retained for 90 days. This satisfies the GDPR data minimization principle while preserving enough history for debugging and audit trails. See Log retention for the full policy.

Cipi monitors privileged authentication events via PAM ( pam_exec.so ) and sends real-time email alerts when a user elevates via sudo or su , or when root /sudoers log in via SSH. SSH login notifications include the key fingerprint and comment (resolved by matching the /var/log/auth.log fingerprint against authorized_keys ), so you can immediately identify which key was used to access the server. Email alerts are also sent when SSH keys are added to, removed from, or renamed on the cipi user, and when apps are created, edited, or deleted. Notifications include contextual details (username, TTY, source IP, fingerprint, key comment, key count) and run asynchronously to avoid login delays. All events are also logged to /var/log/cipi/events.log regardless of SMTP. Email alerts require SMTP configured — fails silently otherwise. See Email Notifications for setup.

A default Cipi install has no web interface — no attack surface from an admin panel, and all management happens over SSH as the cipi user using the cipi CLI. The web control panel is strictly opt-in: install it only if you want a browser dashboard. When you do, it runs as an isolated, self-hosted Laravel app confined with open_basedir ; leave it out and there is no web surface at all.

The Nginx default virtual host uses a rewrite rule to serve a minimal "Server Up" page for all requests to unconfigured domains or direct IP access. This reliable catch-all prevents Nginx from exposing its version number in default error pages.

UFW blocks all ports by default except 22, 80, and 443. Fail2ban monitors SSH with progressive banning : a 24-hour base ban that doubles on each repeat offence (7-day cap), with only 3 retries allowed before a ban — since v5.5.0, cipi firewall attempts changes that number in a drop-in that updates never reset. A dedicated recidive jail catches repeat offenders — 3 bans within 24 hours triggers a 7-day block. Use cipi ban list and cipi ban unban to inspect and manage bans from the CLI.

Cipi enables unattended-upgrades during installation, so the underlying Ubuntu system applies security patches automatically — without any manual intervention. Only security-classified updates are installed unattended; major version upgrades require explicit confirmation. PHP packages are excluded from unattended-upgrades and managed by Cipi instead: since v4.7.13 , cipi php upgrade applies security patches to every installed PHP version on demand or every day at 03:30 (weekly on Sundays before v5.6.3 ). See PHP management . You can verify and manage the configuration at any time: # check unattended-upgrades status systemctl status unattended-upgrades # view the upgrade log cat /var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log # force an immediate unattended upgrade run unattended-upgrade --debug --dry-run Automatic reboots after kernel updates are disabled by default to avoid unexpected downtime. If a kernel update requires a reboot, you will see a notice when you log in via SSH. Schedule the reboot at a convenient maintenance window with sudo reboot .

d: UFW rules and Fail2ban bans.
x: cipi firewall Cipi installs UFW with ports 22, 80, and 443 open by default. Cipi installs UFW with ports 22, 80, and 443 open by default. Use the firewall commands to manage additional rules without touching UFW directly. cipi firewall allow 3306 # open a port cipi firewall allow 3306 --from=10.0.0.5 # allow from specific IP cipi firewall allow 3306 --from=10.0.0.0/24 # allow from subnet cipi firewall deny 8080 # block a port cipi firewall list # show all rules # Failed SSH logins before fail2ban bans an address (v5.5.0+) cipi firewall attempts # threshold, counting window, ban time, default or not cipi firewall attempts 5 # ban after 5 failed logins (1–100) cipi firewall attempts default # back to 3

UFW denies all inbound traffic except SSH, HTTP and HTTPS, and fail2ban bans the addresses that keep failing SSH logins. These are the defaults since 4.3.0: Setting Default Failed SSH logins before a ban 3 — cipi firewall attempts changes it Counted over 1 hour Ban 24 hours, longer for each repeat, up to 7 days Repeat offenders ( recidive ) 3 bans in 24 hours → banned for 7 days

Up to 5.4 the only way to change the threshold was to edit /etc/fail2ban/jail.local by hand — a file Cipi owns. Now: The value is written to /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/cipi-attempts.local ( [sshd] maxretry ). fail2ban reads jail.d/*.local after jail.local , so the value wins and no Cipi update resets it. jail.local itself is not edited. The configuration is checked with fail2ban-client -t before the reload. If fail2ban refuses it, the previous state is put back and nothing changes. With fail2ban stopped the value is saved and applies when it starts. Only the sshd jail changes. Window, ban time and the recidive jail stay as they are. 1 is accepted, with a warning: one mistyped password then bans its owner. CLI only (root), logged in cipi.log . cipi compliance report adds the drop-in to its fail2ban evidence. Servers keep the default of 3 until the command is used: the 5.5.0 migration does not touch fail2ban. Since v5.3.0 , once Cloudflare Tunnel carries the traffic, cipi zt lock http can close 80/443 (or allow only Cloudflare's ranges) and cipi zt lock ssh can close 22. cipi zt disable puts the three default rules back.

Inspect and manage Fail2ban bans directly from the CLI. Cipi configures Fail2ban with progressive banning: a 24-hour base ban that doubles on each repeat offence up to a 7-day cap, with max retries reduced to 3 (since v5.5.0 , cipi firewall attempts changes that number). A dedicated recidive jail bans repeat offenders for 7 days after 3 bans within 24 hours. cipi ban list # list all banned IPs, grouped by jail cipi ban unban 203.0.113.42 # unban a specific IP from all jails
Lists every IP currently banned by Fail2ban, grouped by jail (e.g. sshd , recidive ). Useful for a quick security check or before running an unban.

Removes the given IP from all Fail2ban jails at once. Handy when a legitimate user or CI runner gets locked out by mistake. Since v5.2.0 both commands also cover CrowdSec whenever its engine is running. cipi ban list reads .decisions[] out of cscli decisions list -o json , which returns alerts : reading .value at the top level printed a decision count and then no addresses at all. And cipi ban unban now asks before it claims success, because cscli decisions delete exits 0 whether it removed something or nothing. Existing installations are upgraded automatically by the 4.3.0 migration script when you run cipi self-update . No manual configuration is needed.

d: Add, list and remove admin SSH keys.
x: Manage the authorized SSH keys for the cipi user — the admin SSH entry point. The cipi user (group cipi-ssh ) uses public-key only; root login is disabled. App users (group cipi-apps ) connect with password — see SSH as the app user . Since v5.5.0 , cipi ssh apps can keep app users out of SSH and SFTP, one app or all of them. Commands cipi ssh list # list all authorized keys with fingerprint, comment, and current-session marker cipi ssh add [key] # add a new SSH public key (validates format, prevents duplicates) cipi ssh remove [n] # remove a key by number cipi ssh rename [n] [name] # change t

cipi ssh list # list all authorized keys with fingerprint, comment, and current-session marker cipi ssh add [key] # add a new SSH public key (validates format, prevents duplicates) cipi ssh remove [n] # remove a key by number cipi ssh rename [n] [name] # change the display name / comment of a key # Structured output (v5.0.6+) — panel API cipi ssh list --json REST: GET|POST /api/ssh/keys , DELETE /api/ssh/keys/{n} (API 1.15.0+ / Cipi 5.0.6+ ).

cipi ssh remove includes two safeguards to prevent lockout: Current-session protection — you cannot remove the key used by your active SSH session. Last-key protection — you cannot remove the last remaining authorized key.

SSH keys are stored with their original comments intact, making it easy to identify who each key belongs to. Use cipi ssh rename to change the display name of any key: # list keys to find the number cipi ssh list # rename key #2 cipi ssh rename 2 "john-macbook"

When SMTP is configured, Cipi sends an email alert every time a key is added, removed, or renamed. The notification includes the server hostname, IP address, key fingerprint, key comment, timestamp, and remaining key count. Rename notifications also include the old and new key name.

h: cipi ssh apps — SSH/SFTP access of app users (v5.5.0+, the server's keys since v5.9.0)
x: Every app has its own Linux user. Since 5.9.0 the server's SSH keys — the ones of the cipi user, managed with the key commands above — open a shell as any app user: ssh shop@server , with the key you already use, whatever the app's own setting. sshd reads them at every login, so a key removed with cipi ssh remove stops working for the apps in the same moment. What an app accepts besides those keys — its password, over SSH and SFTP, and its own ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — is the switch below, for one app or for all of them: cipi ssh apps # every app user: enabled or disabled, and what new apps get cipi ssh apps --json cipi ssh apps disable shop # from outside: the server's keys, nothing else cipi ssh apps enable shop # also its password (SSH, SFTP) and its own keys cipi ssh apps sync # rewrite Cipi's section of sshd_config (v5.9.0+) cipi ssh apps disable --all # every app user, and the apps created from now on cipi ssh apps enable --all # everyone back, whatever the single settings were Disabled means: from another machine, the server's keys and nothing else — no password, no key of the app's own. (Before 5.9.0 it meant no login from outside at all.) Logins from the server itself stay as they were, because Deployer reaches the app user over ssh localhost : deploys, webhooks and rollbacks keep working. Sessions already open stay open until they close. --all changes every app user, whatever the single settings were, and sets what apps created afterwards get ( cipi app create , cipi sync import ). After a disable --all , single users can still be enabled one by one. How. The state

d: AES-256 encryption at rest for configs, tokens and keys.
x: Cipi encrypts all configuration files at rest using AES-256-CBC . The Vault system provides transparent encryption and decryption so that sensitive data — database passwords, API tokens, SSH keys, .env contents — is never stored in plaintext on disk. Architecture The system is built on two layers: Vault — transparent encryption of JSON configuration files on disk ( server.json , apps.json , databases.json , backup.json , smtp.json , api.json ) Sync encryption — passphrase-based encryption of export archives for secure transfer between servers How Vault works A master key is generated during in

The system is built on two layers: Vault — transparent encryption of JSON configuration files on disk ( server.json , apps.json , databases.json , backup.json , smtp.json , api.json ) Sync encryption — passphrase-based encryption of export archives for secure transfer between servers

A master key is generated during installation with openssl rand -base64 32 and stored at /etc/cipi/.vault_key ( chmod 400 , root-only). Every JSON config file is encrypted on disk with openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pbkdf2 . Files keep the .json extension — the content is simply an encrypted blob instead of readable JSON. The vault_read function auto-detects whether a file is plaintext or encrypted (backward compatibility), so existing servers migrate seamlessly during update.

# Core functions in lib/vault.sh vault_init # Generate .vault_key if not present vault_read <file> # Decrypt and output JSON to stdout (auto-detect plain/encrypted) vault_write <file> # Read JSON from stdin, encrypt and write to disk vault_seal <file> # Encrypt an existing plaintext file in-place vault_get <file> <jq_query> # Shortcut: vault_read | jq

Cipi generates an apps-public.json file containing only non-sensitive fields (domain, aliases, PHP version, branch, repository, user, creation timestamp, plus suspended and basic_auth flags). The cipi-api group reads this plaintext projection instead of the encrypted file, keeping the vault key restricted to root.

When you run cipi sync export , configs are decrypted from the vault into a staging area, then the entire archive is encrypted with your passphrase. On import, the archive is decrypted with the passphrase, and configs are re-encrypted with the destination server's vault key . If the vault key is lost, configuration files become irrecoverable. The key is protected by chmod 400 and included in server backups. Consider exporting it manually for additional safety.

d: Opt-in IP reputation and community blocklists.
x: Available since v5.2.0 , and off by default : neither setup.sh nor cipi self-update installs it. CrowdSec reads your Nginx logs, decides which IPs are attacking, and a firewall bouncer drops them. It is not a WAF — no request is inspected or rewritten in flight, and fail2ban stays exactly where it is. cipi crowdsec enable # engine + firewall bouncer cipi crowdsec status # engine / bouncer / rescue / decisions cipi crowdsec allow 203.0.113.42 # never ban this address cipi crowdsec unallow 203.0.113.42 # drop an extra allow cipi crowdsec rescue token # print the break-glass curl (on-box) cipi cr

The engine and crowdsec-firewall-bouncer-nftables (or the -iptables variant), registered with cscli bouncers add . That pairing is the whole point: decisions without a bouncer ban nothing at all. On Ubuntu 24.04 iptables is nft underneath, so the bouncer lands on the same plane as fail2ban's iptables-multiport . Acquisition reads /home/*/logs/nginx-{access,error}.log , which is where every Cipi vhost actually writes. /var/log/nginx alone holds only the catch-all server block, so the nginx scenarios would never see a single line of application traffic.

Below 512MB free RAM. The engine plus the bouncer needs headroom you do not have. Nginx looks like it sits behind a reverse proxy without set_real_ip_from and real_ip_header . Every log line would carry your CDN's address, so CrowdSec would ban Cloudflare and leave the attacker alone. --force overrides it if you know better. Since v5.3.0 the error points at cipi zt enable , which writes exactly that Cloudflare real_ip config. Before anything can start banning, enable allowlists the SSH session you are typing from . And cipi crowdsec disable flushes the CrowdSec chains and tables first, then purges : removing the packages while DROP rules are still loaded would leave bans that outlive cscli — and nothing left to lift them with.

Automatic banning and remote administration are one bad decision away from each other, so enable also starts a TLS server on a high port. One GET carrying a one-shot token allowlists the TCP peer — never X-Forwarded-For — unbans that address in CrowdSec and fail2ban, mails you a new token, and then the token dies. It is not a login and not an SSH key: it buys back the ability to connect, nothing more. UFW opens the port, and an ACCEPT is punched at the head of the CrowdSec chain — and punched again on every bouncer restart — so a DROP-all ban cannot close the door behind you. The TLS handshake runs in the connection's own thread with a deadline, never inside accept() : wrapping the listening socket would let a single peer that connects and then says nothing hold the break-glass path shut for as long as it likes. Concurrent connections are capped below the unit's TasksMax . cipi crowdsec status shows the port and the certificate fingerprint — never the token. The throttle applies to wrong tokens only : a correct token is always honoured, whatever the peer typed before it.

Shipped so that your own infrastructure never bans itself: Localhost, RFC1918 ranges, and Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 validation. GitHub webhook CIDRs , pulled from the .hooks key of api.github.com/meta . The fetch is fail-open: if it dies, the previous file stays in place. GitLab.com egress CIDRs , hardcoded and dated 2026-09-07 . They are documented as rotting, because they will. Anything you add yourself with cipi crowdsec allow <ip|cidr> . cipi ban list and cipi ban unban now include CrowdSec whenever the engine is up, so there is one place to look and one place to lift a ban. CrowdSec runs 24/7 once enabled — unlike cipi scan , which is the nightly job. cipi status lists the engine, its bouncer and the rescue listener only when those units exist: a rescue listener that has stopped is the one thing you want to notice before you need it.

The listener runs as root — redeeming a token needs it — but with NoNewPrivileges , ProtectHome=read-only , PrivateTmp and a MemoryHigh cap. ProtectSystem and SystemCallFilter are deliberately left off: hardening that can break the break-glass path is worse than the surface it removes. Migration 5.2.0 installs cipi-scan-manifest and the two rescue helpers, creates the manifest store, grants every existing app its manifest sudo entry, and adds SSH_CLIENT / SSH_CONNECTION to env_keep in /etc/sudoers.d/cipi-sudo . That last one matters: setup.sh sets PermitRootLogin no , so the normal path is sudo cipi , and sudo's env_reset was dropping the only variables that carry the operator's IP. The candidate file is validated with visudo -c before it replaces the live one. Nothing else is migrated: CrowdSec and the scan stay off.

d: Reach SSH through Cloudflare and close port 22.
x: Available since v5.3.0 , and off until you ask — the same contract as CrowdSec : setup.sh and cipi self-update never install cloudflared and never call cipi zt enable . Fail2ban and UFW stay; this feature teaches them about Cloudflare rather than replacing them. Public sites stay public — visitors of a shop go through Cloudflare's CDN/WAF over the same tunnel, with no login. Staging, the GUI and SSH are what you put behind Cloudflare Access. Every step that could cut you off is a separate, explicit command. # 1 — API token, saved root-only cipi zt token set --token=CF_API_TOKEN --account=ACCOU

cipi zt token set stores the token root-only at /etc/cipi/zt.token . If --account is omitted and the token sees exactly one account, Cipi uses it. The token needs Account · Cloudflare Tunnel: Edit , Account · Access: Apps and Policies: Edit and Zone · DNS: Edit ; Origin CA also needs Zone · SSL and Certificates: Edit . This is not /etc/cipi/cloudflare.ini . That file belongs to certbot's DNS-01 challenge ( cipi ssl dns set ) and needs Zone.DNS only. The two credentials stay separate.

h: What enable does — and what it leaves alone
x: Installs the official cloudflared package and runs a locally-managed tunnel under its own systemd unit. Writes Nginx real_ip from https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/ips , reading CF-Connecting-IP ( /etc/nginx/conf.d/cipi-cloudflare-realip.conf ), so logs, fail2ban and your app see the visitor instead of Cloudflare. Adds the same ranges to fail2ban's ignoreip as a backup and, when CrowdSec is already on, to a CrowdSec allowlist. Installs a daily cipi zt refresh cron. A failed fetch keeps the previous list. Does not close 22, 80 or 443.

Command What it does cipi zt hostname add <app|--gui> CNAME to {tunnel-id}.cfargotunnel.com , ingress http://127.0.0.1:80 . Public — CDN/WAF, no Access. cipi app create does not do this on its own; cipi zt status lists the apps that are not on the tunnel yet. cipi zt hostname remove <app|--gui> Removes the DNS records and Access applications Cipi created for it, and the ingress rule. cipi zt access enable <app|--gui> Cloudflare Access in front of that hostname, allowing any authenticated user — tighten the identity provider in the Zero Trust dashboard. If the app has a Git webhook, a Bypass application is created for /cipi/webhook so GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are not answered with a 403. cipi zt access disable <app|--gui> Drops Access; the hostname stays public on the tunnel. cipi zt ssh enable --hostname= Ingress ssh://127.0.0.1:22 plus an Access SSH application, then prints the ~/.ssh/config block below. Port 22 stays open. cipi zt ssh disable Removes SSH from the tunnel — reopening port 22 first if it was locked. # ~/.ssh/config on your laptop Host ssh.example.com ProxyCommand cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h User cipi IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 Deployer still SSHs to localhost , so deploys are not affected by any of this.

cipi zt lock http [--yes] refuses while any app still renews Let's Encrypt over HTTP-01 : validation does not come from Cloudflare's IPs, so those certificates would quietly stop renewing. Move each app to cipi ssl install <app> --dns=cloudflare or cipi zt origin-cert <app> first; --force skips the check if you accept the consequence. Then: if every HTTP hostname — the GUI included — is on the tunnel, 80/443 are closed entirely: the origin goes dark; otherwise 80/443 are allowed only from Cloudflare's ranges , kept current by the daily refresh. cipi zt lock ssh [--yes] closes port 22 only if cloudflared is active and the tunnel already has SSH ingress ; otherwise it would lock you out. The way back is cipi zt ssh unlock . A CrowdSec rescue listener, if enabled, stays reachable. Lock SSH only after ssh ssh.example.com through cloudflared already works from your own machine. If the tunnel stops while port 22 is closed, the way in is your VPS provider's console — keep it at hand before you run lock ssh .

cipi zt origin-cert <app> requests a 15-year Cloudflare Origin CA certificate for the app's domains, stores it under /etc/ssl/cipi-origin/<app>/ and swaps the ssl_certificate paths when the vhost already has a :443 block. The app is marked so a later cipi ssl install over HTTP-01 will not overwrite it. It is not a default replacement for Let's Encrypt. Full (Strict) still needs an origin certificate, but the tunnel talks HTTP to :80 and does not need one.

h: How it fits the rest of Cipi
x: cipi ssl install over HTTP-01 refuses while lock http is on, and on an app with an Origin CA certificate. Apps on the tunnel get certbot --no-redirect , and cipi ssl force refuses on them: an origin HTTP→HTTPS redirect would break cloudflared . CrowdSec's reverse-proxy check still refuses without real_ip ; the error now points at cipi zt enable , after which the check finds the Cloudflare config. Notification triggers: zt_enable , zt_disable , zt_lock_http and zt_lock_ssh . The panel API sudoers grant cipi zt status only. enable , lock and everything else stay with the operator on the CLI. cipi zt disable reopens UFW 22/80/443, removes the Access applications and DNS records Cipi created, deletes the tunnel, purges cloudflared and removes the real_ip, fail2ban and CrowdSec files and the cron. Fail2ban stays, and your Let's Encrypt certificates are left alone.

d: Nightly scans of app files.
x: Available since v5.2.0 , and off by default . It answers one question: did anything change in this app that no deploy put there? A nightly run at 04:40 checks integrity first, then hands the upload directories to ClamAV. cipi scan enable # nightly integrity + upload ClamAV cipi scan # run it now, every app cipi scan myapp # one app now cipi scan status # enabled? signatures? cipi scan report # the last report cipi scan manifest myapp # rewrite the integrity manifest cipi scan disable # remove the scanner and its cron Integrity, then antivirus The integrity pass compares current/ (or htdocs/ fo

The integrity pass compares current/ (or htdocs/ for custom apps) against a sha256 manifest written at every successful deploy and rollback . Then one ClamAV process runs over the upload directories only , with the rfxn PHP-webshell signatures added. Scanning a whole release tree nightly buys noise, not safety — the manifest already covers everything a deploy put there.

h: Where the manifests live, and why
x: In /var/lib/cipi/manifests , root:root 0600 — never in the app home. open_basedir gives PHP all of /home/<app>/ , so a manifest kept there would be editable by the very webshell the check exists to catch. The webhook deploy runs as the app user, so it reaches the manifest writer through one sudo entry pinned to its own app name . Every re-baseline is written to events.log : a manifest rewrite with no deploy beside it is exactly the thing to look for.

h: Filenames that used to hide a webshell
x: Comparison slices sha256sum records by offset instead of splitting on whitespace. Names containing spaces were being truncated in the report, and GNU coreutils escapes any record holding a backslash or a newline — which a hash-anchored filter dropped entirely. A webshell called sh\ell.php was invisible.

scan_integrity — extra or changed files. FPM open_basedir and pool-user drift are reported in the same mail. scan_incomplete — timeouts, failed signature updates, or a release that could not be hashed in full. It is deliberately not called “clean”: a check that did not finish has told you nothing.

cipi scan enable refuses below 2GB free RAM or 3GB free on /var ( --force overrides). clamscan loads the entire signature set on every run, and an OOM kill at 04:40 may take MariaDB down with it. Read the limits honestly. The check tells you a tree changed between deploys. An attacker who owns the app user can still re-baseline through the sudo entry — which is why every re-baseline is logged, and why you read events.log alongside the alert. Per-app Unix users and open_basedir were already Cipi's isolation model; this only verifies it is still in place. A pre-symlink checkpoint and inotify on uploads are not in this release.

d: ISO 27001 and SOC 2 checks and reports.
x: Available since v5.3.1 . Cipi cannot be ISO 27001 or SOC 2 certified: there is no organisation or service to audit, only software on your server. What a team under audit needs is evidence that the deploy platform meets the controls, in a form the auditor accepts. cipi compliance collects it. It is read-only : no check changes the server, runs apt update or writes config. Nothing is installed, scheduled or enabled. cipi compliance # all 17 controls: pass / warn / fail / info / n/a cipi compliance tls --days=30 # one control, custom period cipi compliance --json # exits 1 on any fail — gate CI o

cipi compliance report writes /var/log/cipi/compliance/<host>-<UTC time>/ : report.md — for the auditor; report.json — for tooling; evidence/<control>/… — the raw command output behind each finding (since 5.4.0 deploys adds deploy-audit.jsonl , deploy-audit.tsv , deploy-audit-chain.txt , deploy-audit-hooks.txt and deploy-audit-unaudited.tsv next to deploys.tsv ); SHA256SUMS , plus a .tar.gz of the directory and its .sha256 . Everything is root-only (700/600). The command prints the archive's SHA-256: record it outside the server , so the bundle can later be shown to be unaltered. Each run is logged to cipi.log . --days (default 90) sets the look-back period for tokens, deploys and logs.

Mapped to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A and the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria; cipi compliance controls prints the exact mapping. Control What it checks ssh Effective sshd -T configuration firewall ufw active with default deny intrusion fail2ban jails, CrowdSec patching unattended-upgrades, pending security updates (from the cached lists), reboot-required kernel CIS network sysctls tls nginx -T protocols, HSTS, Let's Encrypt expiry and key type accounts UID 0, empty passwords, accounts not managed by Cipi, sudoers ssh_keys Fingerprints; RSA under 3072 bits and DSA flagged api_tokens No expiry, expired, unused for the period, * ability, IP allowlist * gui_2fa Two-factor authentication on GUI accounts secrets Encrypted, root-only config; key file modes deploys Since 5.4.0, the deploy audit ledger : fails on a broken hash chain; warns when an app's deploy.php lacks the audit hook, its sudoers lacks the rule, or Deployer's releases_log has a release the ledger never saw. Only releases since auditing began count. Without the ledger (not yet updated) it warns instead of passing backups Schedule freshness, off-site copy, encryption logging Remote forwarding, auth.log history, journald, auditd monitoring Monitor cron, disabled checks, alert delivery, muted triggers time NTP synchronisation malware cipi scan

Panel SQLite databases are read as their owner with sqlite3 -readonly (PHP PDO fallback), selecting named columns only. Token hashes, password hashes and 2FA secrets are never selected. SSH keys are exported as fingerprints, and backup credentials are not exported. Honest about gaps. secrets is at best a warn: the vault uses AES-256-CBC without a MAC, which is not authenticated encryption, and the report says so before an auditor has to ask. backups notes that restore tests are not recorded. deploys states that the hash chain proves nothing before the newest record was changed or removed, but root can still rewrite the newest records or the whole file — the syslog copy forwarded off the server is the independent one. Cipi's own design choices appear as notes, not failures: password SFTP login for cipi-apps users, and nginx, databases and PHP kept off unattended-upgrades .

d: Add cipi-agent to a Laravel app.
x: Cipi Agent ( cipi/agent on Packagist ) is the official Laravel companion for Cipi . It bridges your application and the server control panel with: Webhook-triggered deploys from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea and Azure DevOps, recorded in the deploy audit ledger Health monitoring (app, database, cache, queue with failed jobs, storage, live release and commit) An in-app MCP server for AI assistants (Cursor, VS Code, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, any MCP client) — 11 tools plus optional panel tools cipi.yml tooling — validate, inspect and generate the declarative server configuration with the s

Requirement Version PHP 8.3+ Laravel 12 or 13 Database (anonymizer) MySQL / MariaDB or PostgreSQL CLI tools (anonymizer) mysqldump (or mariadb-dump ) / pg_dump on the server Optional cipi/sdk ^1.0 for the panel tools , ext-zlib for gzip dumps composer require cipi/agent The service provider auto-discovers — no config/app.php change is needed. composer require cipi/agent:^2.0 . Existing MCP clients, webhooks, health monitors and the anonymizer API keep working unchanged. Behaviour that did change: password transformation now sets every row to the hash of options.password (default password ), computed once, instead of re-hashing the stored hash — the anonymized copy is finally usable for login. Set options.password if you relied on a specific value. Health no longer reports degraded when deploy metadata is missing or the last automatic deploy failed (the previous release is still live); the information is in checks.deploy . Deploy trigger file gained source , actor , ip , ref and request_id for the audit ledger; the 1.x keys are still written. db_query additionally blocks ALTER , RENAME , CREATE … , administrative statements and multi-statement input; CIPI_MCP_DB_WRITE=false makes it read-only. artisan additionally blocks db:wipe , migrate:fresh , migrate:reset , pail and horizon:* . The agent exposes a POST endpoint at /cipi/webhook . When your Git provider sends a push event, the agent verifies the signature and writes a .deploy-trigger file. The app user's crontab (installed by Cipi) picks it up within a minute, moves it aside and runs cipi-app-deploy , which wraps Deployer: clone, composer install , migrations, symlink swap, worker restart, cipi.yml reconciliation, post-deploy steps and the post-deploy healthcheck. A GitHub ping answers pong ; events that are not a push (pull requests, tags on Bitbucket, …) are acknowledged with 202 ignored . This design means the webhook response is instant (no HTTP timeout waiting for deployment to complete) and Deployer runs with the correct user permissions — no sudo required.

Custom setups can also send ?token= or a Bearer token. The token to use is stored in .env as CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN . You can also retrieve it any time with: cipi deploy myapp --webhook

Only a push to the branch named in .env deploys: CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH=main Pushes to any other branch receive a skipped response and no deploy is triggered (since 2.1.0 the webhook answer also names the app's environment). Without the key, every push deploys. Since Cipi 5.7.2 the key is written at cipi app create with the app's deploy branch and kept in step by cipi app edit --branch and cipi sync import ; migration 5.7.2 adds it to existing Laravel apps that lack it and leaves a value already there alone. Since 5.8.0 a deploy.branch applied from cipi.yml rewrites it too, and the app's environment label sits next to it as CIPI_ENV .

Since 2.0 the trigger file carries what the payload said about the push — provider, actor (pusher), commit, delivery id and the client IP — in the format cipi-app-deploy reads: {"source":"github","actor":"octocat","ip":"140.82.115.3","ref":"main@abcdef123456","request_id":"8d2f…"} Cipi stores these under claimed in the root-owned, hash-chained deploy audit ledger ( cipi deploy <app> --audit ), next to the facts root establishes on its own (release, commit, process chain). The MCP deploy tool writes the same file with source: mcp and the actor the assistant was given, so every deploy says who asked for it.

The Bearer token is resolved in order: CIPI_HEALTH_TOKEN (dedicated), then CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN (fallback). Disable the endpoint entirely with php artisan cipi:service health --disable or CIPI_HEALTH_CHECK=false .

d: Validate and generate cipi.yml from your app.
x: cipi.yml is the declarative file committed with the app that drives its server configuration: PHP version, aliases, php.ini overrides, limits, basic auth, extra databases, workers (queues, Horizon, Reverb), scheduler, healthcheck, deploy recipe (the deploy branch too, since Cipi 5.8.0) and post-deploy steps, redirects, proxies, SSL, required .env names, crons and backup profiles. On the server, cipi yml validate | plan | apply reconcile it — reading, since Cipi 5.8.0 , a cipi-<env>.yml for the app's environment before cipi.yml , so one repository can carry a staging and a production file. Sinc

cipi yml generate <app> on the server prints what is configured today . php artisan cipi:yml generate is the other direction — a starting point derived from the code for an app that has never run on Cipi: Horizon or plain queue workers ( QUEUE_CONNECTION ), Reverb, Scout with Meilisearch, scheduled tasks, the /up health route, CIPI_PHP_VERSION , extra databases in the app's namespace and the credential-looking keys of .env.example for env.required . Everything else is left as commented examples. The output is run through the validator before it is returned, so it is never a file the server would reject.

Unknown keys, values outside their bounds, databases or backup profiles outside the app's namespace, forbidden runners in deploy.post — every rule the server applies is applied here, with the same path: message output. The validator also reads the local .env and warns about each env.required name that is missing or empty, because the server blocks the plan while one is. Namespace rules need the app name: CIPI_APP_USER , or --app=<name> outside the server. php artisan cipi:yml validate INFO cipi.yml is valid (/var/www/shop/cipi.yml) WARN env.required: STRIPE_KEY is not set in .env — the server blocks the plan while it is missing See what applying it would change on the server: cipi yml plan shop

cipi:yml schema --write publishes cipi.schema.json (JSON Schema 2020-12, also available with vendor:publish --tag=cipi-schemas ). Point the YAML language server at it with a first-line comment and get completion and inline errors while you type: # yaml-language-server: $schema=./cipi.schema.json version: 1

The MCP cipi_yml tool runs the same actions ( validate , show , generate , example ) and accepts a draft as content , so an AI assistant can propose a change, validate it and hand you a file the server accepts — without writing to the repository itself. The env_check tool reports which env.required names are missing on the server, with no values. The local validator and the server validator are the same schema. When a Cipi release adds a cipi.yml key — deploy.branch in 5.8.0, known to the agent since 2.1.0 — or a value, like php: "8.6" in 5.9.1, known to the agent since 2.1.1 — update cipi/agent as well so php artisan cipi:yml validate knows it; until then the server remains authoritative.

It supports MySQL / MariaDB and PostgreSQL (since 2.0 the pg_dump output is streamed through its COPY blocks and INSERT statements), uses Faker -based transformations configured via a JSON file, and runs as a background job so large databases do not block HTTP requests. The real data never lingers: the original dump is deleted as soon as it has been processed, outputs are 0600 , and d

Local development — give every developer a realistic dataset without copying production emails, addresses, or payment notes Staging / preview environments — refresh a non-production database from production structure and volume, with PII replaced QA and demos — reproduce bugs that depend on relational data without GDPR risk Vendor or contractor access — share a SQL dump when a full VPN + production access is not acceptable Developer laptops — cipi-cli db anonymize myapp --email you@example.com requests a dump through the Cipi API, with no SSH session and no token to copy around (see From your laptop with cipi-cli ) CI pipelines — run cipi:anonymize on the server or trigger POST /cipi/db from a secure automation step

Use the agent anonymizer when people need data that looks real but must not contain real identities. You can use both on the same project: backup for ops, anonymize for humans.

An authenticated POST /cipi/db request (with a recipient email , optionally gzip ) validates anonymization.json and queues AnonymizeDatabaseJob The job dumps the database with mysqldump or pg_dump --format=plain (password via MYSQL_PWD / PGPASSWORD , never on the command line) streams the dump: MySQL extended INSERT s are tokenized value by value, PostgreSQL COPY … FROM stdin blocks field by field — only the columns listed in anonymization.json are rewritten, the rows of truncate tables are dropped, everything else is copied byte for byte deletes the original dump, writes storage/cipi/anonymized_{jobId}.sql ( .sql.gz with gzip) with permissions 0600 On success, Laravel sends an email with a time-limited download URL ( CIPI_ANONYMIZER_TTL , default 15 minutes) and a summary: size, rows transformed per table, tables emptied, warnings GET /cipi/db/{token} serves the file — no Bearer token; the signed URL itself is the credential On failure, a plain-text error email is sent to the same address The sequence is the same whichever client sends the request — curl , a CI job, or cipi-cli db anonymize : the client only changes who assembles the URL and the token.

The HTTP API does not return the download URL in the JSON response — email is the only delivery channel for POST /cipi/db . Understanding who receives it and what must be configured avoids silent failures. Who receives the email? Exactly the address you pass in the JSON body — nothing else: { "email" : "developer@example.com" } Success → HTML email with the signed download link (15 minutes) Failure → plain-text email with the error and job ID No CC, BCC, or fallback to the Cipi admin, CIPI_APP_USER , or a fixed address in .env Whoever holds CIPI_ANONYMIZER_TOKEN chooses the recipient on each request Laravel mail must work Notifications use Laravel's Mail facade and your application's MAIL_* settings — the same config as password resets or contact forms. This is independent of Cipi server SMTP ( cipi smtp configure for backup/deploy alerts on the host). The panel uses classic session login and supports optional TOTP two-factor authentication . Each administrator can enrol an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, 1Password, Aegis, …) from their profile. 2FA is opt-in per user, not forced. Existing accounts — seeded by cipi gui , created from an invite link — are matched by their email (case-insensitive) and linked to the provider's identity ( users.sso_subject ) on the first sign-in; from then on the link wins, so a renamed mailbox still lands on the same account. An email already linked to a different identity is refused (“linked to another identity”). New people get an account only when their email domain is in --domains ; everyone else sees “No panel account for … Ask an admin for an invite link.” Nothing is created for a refused sign-in. Roles and grants are the panel's, as before: an auto-created account is a user with nothing granted; admins hand out servers and apps in Team, where SSO-linked accounts carry an SSO badge. MFA: the identity provider is the authority — the panel's own TOTP step is skipped after an SSO sign-in. Password sign-ins keep their TOTP as before. Under the hood: authorization-code flow with PKCE (S256), state and nonce ; the code is exchanged server-to-server with the client secret; the identity comes from the provider's userinfo endpoint , and the ID token's issuer, audience and nonce are checked against the handshake. An email_verified: false claim is refused; a provider that does not send the claim (Entra ID) is accepted. Where it shows: Settings → Panel has a read-only Single sign-on card for admins (status, provider, SSO-only, auto-provisioned domains, the redirect URI to copy, and the CLI to change it); the panel's own .env keys are CIPI_GUI_SSO_ISSUER , _CLIENT_ID , _CLIENT_SECRET , _LABEL , _DOMAINS , _ONLY , _SCOPES .

SSO-only and a broken provider: from the server, cipi gui sso only off brings password sign-in back, cipi gui sso disable turns SSO off altogether, cipi gui reset-user resets the admin account. The API is not installed inside an app. It is a separate Laravel application with its own Nginx vhost and its own certificate, so it needs a domain or subdomain that only the API uses . h: Changing the API domain — cipi api move
x: Installed the API on the wrong domain, or rebranding? Move it. The Laravel app, tokens, job history and IP whitelist stay exactly as they are; only the address changes. cipi api move api.newdomain.com # move and issue the new certificate cipi api move api.newdomain.com --no-ssl # move now, certificate later (cipi api ssl) Point the new domain at the server first (DNS A / AAAA record): Let's Encrypt checks it over port 80. cipi api move rewrites the Nginx vhost for the new domain. If nginx -t rejects it, the old vhost goes back and nothing else changes. It updates /etc/cipi/api.json and APP_URL , and restarts cipi-queue . SSL: it deletes the old domain's certificate, including any -0001 copies certbot made, so nothing renews a domain the server no longer serves. Then it issues a certificate for the new domain. If that fails (DNS not propagated yet, port 80 closed), the API is already on the new domain over HTTP: fix the cause and run cipi api ssl . A certificate that an app still uses is never deleted. Then update the URL in every client of the server: the server's entry in the GUI (Connections), the cipi-cli profile, the PHP SDK configuration and MCP clients ( https://api.newdomain.com/mcp ). Tokens keep working. Running cipi api <other-domain> on a server whose API is already configured stops and points you to cipi api move . Before 5.7.0 it silently changed domain, lost the HTTPS configuration and left the old certificate renewing.

h: Removing the API — cipi api remove
x: Uninstalls everything cipi api <domain> set up. Your apps, databases and the GUI are untouched. uninstall is an alias, and --force skips the confirmation. cipi api remove cipi api remove --force It removes: the cipi-queue worker the Nginx vhost and the PHP-FPM pool the scheduler, maintenance and nightly update crons the Let's Encrypt certificate of the API domain /opt/cipi/api , /opt/cipi/api.old and the upgrade backups api.json , the IP whitelist and the API logs All tokens die with it, so GUI panels, cipi-cli and MCP clients that use this server lose access. The www-data sudoers whitelist ( /etc/sudoers.d/cipi-api ) stays, because it is part of every Cipi install. Reinstall any time with cipi api <domain> : you get a new, empty token database.

A profile is a named connection to one Cipi server (API endpoint + token). Use as many profiles as you have servers — for example prod , staging , or client-a . You need the API endpoint URL and a Sanctum token created with cipi api token create on each server. Credentials are stored per profile in ~/.cipi/config.json with permissions 0600 . Always pass a profile name — if you omit it, the CLI prompts for one instead of silently writing to default .

Recommended: store the token with api token add . Equivalent helpers are configure --profile and profiles add : cipi-cli api token add prod Cipi API endpoint: https://api.example.com API token: 1|yourtoken... Server profile "prod" saved → ~/.cipi/config.json cipi-cli api token add staging Cipi API endpoint: https://staging-api.example.com API token: 1|stagingtoken... Server profile "staging" saved → ~/.cipi/config.json # Same flow via configure / profiles add cipi-cli configure --profile prod cipi-cli profiles add staging
cipi-cli api token add prod \ --endpoint https://api.example.com --token "1|yourtoken..." cipi-cli profiles add staging \ --endpoint https://staging.example.com --token "1|yourtoken..."
cipi-cli profiles show prod Profile: prod Endpoint: https://api.example.com Token: 1|a8Kz...4f2a cipi-cli profiles show # Shows all configured server profiles

Manage multiple server connections from a single cipi-cli installation. One profile equals one server. Prefix any command with a profile name to target that server, or set a default with profiles use to omit the prefix. The aliases servers / server work the same as profiles .

Aliases: servers / server → profiles ; profiles use → profiles default . List every primary domain and alias across all apps on the server in a single table — the remote counterpart to cipi domains on the server. Useful for auditing DNS coverage or spotting domains missing SSL before a certificate renewal. Command Description cipi-cli domains List every domain and alias across all apps cipi-cli domains DOMAIN APP KIND TYPE PHP SSL api.myapp.com myapp alias Laravel 8.5 ✓ myapp.com myapp primary Laravel 8.5 ✓ www.myapp.com myapp alias Laravel 8.5 ✓ 3 domains · 1 app · 3 certificates The global domain map is built from GET /api/apps on the server. Trigger deployments, rollback to the previous release, or unlock a stuck deployment. Command Description cipi-cli deploy <app> Trigger a zero-downtime deployment cipi-cli deploy rollback <app> [-y] Rollback to previous release cipi-cli deploy unlock <app> Unlock a stuck deployment cipi-cli deploy config show|set <app> Read or update structured deploy.php options (Cipi 5.0.3+) cipi-cli deploy audit <app> [--days N] Deploy audit ledger: origin, operator, IP and commit of every deploy (Cipi 5.4.0+) cipi-cli yml <app> The app's cipi.yml : file, validity, auto-apply and what applying would change (Cipi 5.6.4+); the environment and the cipi-<env>.yml in use (cipi-cli 1.9.0+, Cipi 5.8.0+) cipi-cli yml apply <app> Apply the committed cipi.yml as an async job (Cipi 5.6.4+) cipi-cli yml auto <app> on|off|status Apply cipi.yml after every successful deploy, or stop (Cipi 5.6.4+) deploy config set flags: --keep-releases N , --migrate , --optimize , --storage-link , --queue-restart , --horizon-terminate , --predeploy-snapshot , --node-build CMD and --extra-artisan CMD (repeatable). The remote counterparts of cipi deploy-config and the deploy audit ledger . The yml commands are the remote side of cipi yml plan | apply | auto . They need API 1.35+ , Cipi 5.6.4+ and a token with yml-view (read) and yml-manage (apply, auto). A token created before 1.35 has neither, so expect a 403 until you issue a new one. Turning auto-apply on asks for confirmation: from then on, anyone who can push to the repository can change the app's server settings. cipi-cli deploy myapp Deploying myapp... Polling jo

Manage MariaDB and PostgreSQL databases on the server, and request anonymized dumps from Laravel apps that run cipi/agent . Aliases: database , dbs → db . Command Description cipi-cli db engines List installed database engines and the server default (Cipi 4.8+) cipi-cli db install <engine> Install an engine: mariadb or pgsql (Cipi 5.0.6+) cipi-cli db list [--engine E] List databases with their size, optionally filtered by engine cipi-cli db create <name> [--engine E] Create a database (MariaDB unless --engine pgsql ) cipi-cli db delete <name> [-y] Delete a database — API < 1.19 only; newer servers use cipi db delete on the host cipi-cli db backup <name> Create a compressed backup on the server cipi-cli db restore <name> [-y] Restore the latest backup (overwrites current data) cipi-cli db password <name> [-y] Regenerate the password and update the linked app .env cipi-cli db anonymize <app> --email <addr> Request an anonymized dump of the app database via cipi/agent (cipi-cli 1.5.0+) cipi-cli db anonymize download <url> [-o file] Download the dump from the signed link received by email cipi-cli db list NAME SIZE myapp 24.5 MB blog 8.2 MB cipi-cli db backup myapp Backup created: myapp_20260402_143022.sql.gz cipi-cli db restore myapp -y Database restored successfully.

The anonymizer is not part of the Cipi API: it lives in the cipi/agent package inside the Laravel app. The CLI reads the app URL ( APP_URL , else https://<primary domain> ) and CIPI_ANONYMIZER_TOKEN from the app .env through the API ( apps-view + apps-env abilities), then calls POST /<CIPI_ROUTE_PREFIX>/db on the app itself. The agent runs the job in the app queue and emails a signed download link valid for 15 minutes. # One-time setup on the app (all through the Cipi API) cipi-cli apps artisan myapp cipi:service anonymize --enable cipi-cli apps artisan myapp cipi:generate-token anonymize cipi-cli apps artisan myapp cipi:init-anonymize # then edit /home/myapp/.db/anonymization.json on the server # Request a dump — the signed link arrives by email cipi-cli prod db anonymize myapp --email dev@example.com ✓ Anonymization job queued for 'myapp' # Download it: default name from the server, -o - streams to stdout cipi-cli db anonymize download "https://myapp.com/cipi/db/<token>?expires=…&signature=…" -o myapp.sql cipi-cli db anonymize download "<signed url>" -o - | mysql -u root myapp_local --email, -e Address that receives the signed download link (prompted when omitted) --url Override the app base URL, e.g. when the app redirects to www — redirects are never followed --token Override the bearer token read from .env --output, -o download : output file ( - for stdout) --force, -f download : overwrite an existing file Requires cipi-cli 1.5.0+ , Cipi 5.0.3+ / API 1.14+ (for apps env ) and cipi/agent 1.1.1+ with the anonymizer enabled in the app. Custom and Node apps are refused. Configure the outgoing email the server uses for notifications — the remote side of email notifications . The stored password is never shown. Requires Cipi 5.0.7+ (API 1.15+) and smtp-view|manage . HTTP healthchecks per app — the remote side of cipi health . Requires Cipi 5.0.7+ (API 1.15+) and health-view|manage .
